'''Richard Montgomery''' (born 1990) is a British mathematician and professor at the [[University of Warwick]]. His research is principally in [[extremal combinatorics|extremal]] and [[probabilistic combinatorics]].<ref name="CV">{{cite web
 | last        = Montgomery
 | first       = Richard
 | title       = Curriculum vitae
 | url         = https://rhmontgomery.warwick.ac.uk/rhmcv.pdf
 | date        = June 2026
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
 | title       = Professor Richard Montgomery
 | url         = https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/Montgomery/
 | publisher   = University of Warwick
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>

== Education and career ==

Montgomery studied at the [[University of Cambridge]], receiving a BA and MMath in 2011 and completing his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 2015 under the supervision of [[Andrew Thomason]]. His thesis was titled ''Minors and Spanning Trees in Graphs''.<ref name="CV" /><ref>{{cite web
 | title       = Richard Montgomery
 | url         = https://mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=284503
 | website     = Mathematics Genealogy Project
 | publisher   = North Dakota State University
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>

He was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of Birmingham]] in 2015 and a [[Junior Research Fellow]] at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], from 2015 to 2019.<ref>{{cite journal
 | title       = Elected into Junior Research Fellowships under Title A
 | journal     = Cambridge University Reporter
 | volume      = 146
 | issue       = 9
 | date        = 18 November 2015
 | page        = 168
 | url         = https://www.admin.cam.ac.uk/reporter/2015-16/weekly/6404/6404.pdf
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref> At Birmingham, he was a Birmingham Fellow from 2018 to 2020, a Senior Birmingham Fellow from 2020 to 2021 and a [[Reader (academic rank)|reader]] in combinatorics from 2021 to 2022. In 2022 he joined the University of Warwick as an associate professor. He became a reader there in 2024 and a full professor in 2025.<ref name="CV" />

== Research ==

Montgomery works on extremal and probabilistic combinatorics, particularly problems concerning subgraphs, [[graph decomposition]]s and [[random graph]]s.<ref>{{cite web
 | title       = Richard Montgomery
 | url         = https://rhmontgomery.warwick.ac.uk/
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>

He resolved a conjecture of [[Jeff Kahn (mathematician)|Jeff Kahn]] about spanning trees in random graphs. Montgomery proved that, for every fixed <math>\Delta>0</math>, there is a constant <math>C=C(\Delta)</math> such that the [[Erdős–Rényi model|binomial random graph]] <math>G(n,C\log n/n)</math> contains a copy of every tree on <math>n</math> vertices with maximum degree at most <math>\Delta</math>, [[with high probability]].<ref name="Spanning">{{cite journal
 | last        = Montgomery
 | first       = Richard
 | title       = Spanning trees in random graphs
 | journal     = [[Advances in Mathematics]]
 | volume      = 356
 | year        = 2019
 | article-number        = 106793
 | doi         = 10.1016/j.aim.2019.106793
 | arxiv       = 1810.03299
}}</ref>

With [[Alexey Pokrovskiy]] and [[Benny Sudakov]], Montgomery studied decompositions of edge-coloured complete bipartite graphs into [[rainbow matching|rainbow perfect matchings]], which correspond to decompositions of [[Latin square]]s into transversals. They also proved that every properly edge-coloured complete graph can be nearly decomposed into rainbow spanning trees.<ref name="Rainbow">{{cite journal
 | last1       = Montgomery
 | first1      = Richard
 | last2       = Pokrovskiy
 | first2      = Alexey
 | last3       = Sudakov
 | first3      = Benny
 | title       = Decompositions into spanning rainbow structures
 | journal     = [[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]]
 | volume      = 119
 | issue       = 4
 | year        = 2019
 | pages       = 899–959
 | doi         = 10.1112/plms.12245
 | arxiv       = 1805.07564
}}</ref>

The same authors proved [[Graceful labeling#Ringel's conjecture|Ringel's conjecture]] for all sufficiently large <math>n</math>. The conjecture, posed by [[Gerhard Ringel]] in 1963, states that, for every tree <math>T</math> with <math>n</math> edges, the edges of the [[complete graph]] <math>K_{2n+1}</math> can be decomposed into <math>2n+1</math> copies of <math>T</math>.<ref name="Ringel">{{cite journal
 | last1       = Montgomery
 | first1      = Richard
 | last2       = Pokrovskiy
 | first2      = Alexey
 | last3       = Sudakov
 | first3      = Benny
 | title       = A proof of Ringel's conjecture
 | journal     = [[Geometric and Functional Analysis]]
 | volume      = 31
 | issue       = 3
 | year        = 2021
 | pages       = 663–720
 | doi         = 10.1007/s00039-021-00576-2
 | arxiv       = 2001.02665
}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine
 | last        = Hartnett
 | first       = Kevin
 | title       = Rainbow Proof Shows Graphs Have Uniform Parts
 | url         = https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematicians-prove-ringels-graph-theory-conjecture-20200219/
 | magazine    = Quanta Magazine
 | date        = 19 February 2020
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>

With Hong Liu, Montgomery solved a problem posed by [[Paul Erdős]] and [[András Hajnal]] in 1981 concerning the odd cycle lengths of graphs with infinite chromatic number. They proved an asymptotically sharp lower bound on the sum of the reciprocals of the odd cycle lengths in a graph in terms of its chromatic number.<ref name="OddCycles">{{cite journal
 | last1       = Liu
 | first1      = Hong
 | last2       = Montgomery
 | first2      = Richard
 | title       = A solution to Erdős and Hajnal's odd cycle problem
 | journal     = [[Journal of the American Mathematical Society]]
 | volume      = 36
 | issue       = 4
 | year        = 2023
 | pages       = 1191–1234
 | doi         = 10.1090/jams/1018
 | arxiv       = 2010.15802
}}</ref>

In 2023, Montgomery proved the Ryser–Brualdi–Stein conjecture for all sufficiently large even <math>n</math>. This conjecture states that every Latin square of even order <math>n</math> has a transversal containing <math>n-1</math> cells.<ref name="RBS">{{cite arXiv
 | last        = Montgomery
 | first       = Richard
 | title       = A proof of the Ryser–Brualdi–Stein conjecture for large even {{mvar|n}}
 | eprint      = 2310.19779
 | class       = math.CO
 | year        = 2023
}}</ref>

== Awards and honours ==

Together with Alexey Pokrovskiy, Montgomery received the 2019 [[European Prize in Combinatorics]]. The prize recognised their "deep contributions to extremal and probabilistic combinatorics".<ref>{{cite web
 | title       = Birmingham Researcher Receives European Prize in Combinatorics
 | url         = https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/news-archive/2019/birmingham-researcher-receives-european-prize-in-combinatorics
 | publisher   = University of Birmingham
 | date        = 8 October 2019
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>

In 2020, Montgomery received a [[Philip Leverhulme Prize]].<ref>{{cite web
 | title       = Philip Leverhulme Prize – Richard Montgomery
 | url         = https://research.birmingham.ac.uk/en/projects/philip-leverhulme-prize-richard-montgomery/
 | publisher   = University of Birmingham
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>

The [[European Mathematical Society]] awarded him an [[European Mathematical Society Prize|EMS Prize]] in 2024, citing his work on Ringel's conjecture, distributive absorption and sublinear expanders.<ref>{{cite web
 | title       = Fourteen prizes awarded to European mathematicians at the 9th ECM
 | url         = https://euromathsoc.org/news/fourteen-prizes-awarded-to-european-mathematicians-at-the-9th-ecm-121
 | publisher   = European Mathematical Society
 | date        = 15 July 2024
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>

In 2025, he received a [[Whitehead Prize]] from the [[London Mathematical Society]] for his work on the absorption method and sublinear expanders in extremal and probabilistic combinatorics.<ref>{{cite web
 | title       = LMS Prize Winners 2025
 | url         = https://www.lms.ac.uk/news/lms-prize-winners-2025
 | publisher   = London Mathematical Society
 | date        = 4 July 2025
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>

In 2026, Montgomery and [[Julian Sahasrabudhe]] jointly received the [[Adams Prize]] for work in discrete mathematics.<ref>{{cite web
 | title       = Adams Prize Winner 2025–26
 | url         = https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/adams-prize/adams-prize-winner-2025-26
 | publisher   = University of Cambridge
 | year        = 2026
 | access-date = 12 August 2026
}}</ref>
